title: Rook pawns: the corner draw and its limits
outcomes: Predicts win or draw in a king-and-rook-pawn ending from Black's king distance to the corner, and says what White's king changes
Tells the rook-pawn draw from the win when the same set-up stands on the b- or c-file
Predicts what a knight adds (a win with the pawn on the fifth rank, a draw with it on the seventh when the knight cannot give mate at once) and sees that a bishop does not change the corner question

steps.text: Pawns on the a- and h-files are special. A rook pawn has only one neighbouring file, so the attacking king can come at it from one side only, and the defending king can wait in the corner in front of it. Watch what a king in the corner can do, then predict.

steps.caption: White to move. Black's king is in the corner on a8. The tablebase gives a draw. One line is shown.

line.say: Black's king stays next to the corner.
Black's king goes back to the corner.
The pawn is blocked, so White must move the king. Kc7 no longer guards a7.
Black takes the pawn. Only the kings are left: a draw.

steps.text: **How close is close enough?** With White's king on b6 and the pawn on a5, Black's king draws from squares close to the corner and loses from farther away. How close depends on White's king too. *Rule of thumb:* count Black's king moves to the corner. Predict, then check.

steps.title: How far from the corner?
steps.prompt: In the first position Black's king is on c8, two king moves from the corner. In the second it is on d8; in the third the position is mirrored onto the h-file, with Black's king on f8. Predict each, then check.

steps.text: **Add a piece.** With a knight, White usually wins a fifth-rank rook pawn against a king in the corner, unless that king is shut in the corner in front of a pawn on the seventh: a *rule of thumb*. A bishop of the wrong colour is a different case with its own, later lesson; here, ask the same question as before: how far is Black's king from the corner?

steps.title: A knight on the board
steps.prompt: In the first position White has a knight on b1 and the pawn is on a5. In the second the pawn has reached a7; in the third the knight stands on d1, not b1. Predict each, then check.
Think back to the three silent positions. What did you check first, and which check would have saved you if you skipped it?
